# Wyrd — full machine-readable reference

> Wyrd is open-source AI assurance and verification infrastructure. Verify AI systems before and after release, with verdicts you can trace, reproduce, and audit.

Every published docs page in sidebar order, generated from the docs content tree. Links are relative to the docs base /wyrd/ (published at https://docs.bohmian.ai/wyrd/). The page index is [llms.txt](/wyrd/llms.txt).

## Start here

Declare -> Observe -> Verify an application you own, in this order. A connected Wyrd MCP server teaches the same route through `wyrd.guide {"topic":"start"}`.

- [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/): run a local server you keep running, and connect MCP hosts.
- [Verify your first agent](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/): declare, observe, and verify the support-desk Service.
- [Error catalog](/wyrd/api/errors/): every stable error code and its remediation.

# What Wyrd verifies

Page: /wyrd/get-started/introduction/

> Wyrd checks that an AI system behaves the way its declaration says it should, before and after deployment.

Wyrd is open-source verification and assurance infrastructure for AI systems. You declare what an AI system should do, record what it actually does, and Wyrd returns a verdict on whether the two match. The system can be an individual LLM, a deployed agent service, or a traditional HTTP service, and the same declaration is checked before release and in production.

This page explains that loop and where Wyrd stops. To run it yourself, start with [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/).

## The verification loop

Wyrd works in three steps, and each one leaves a durable record the next step builds on.

| Step | You provide | Wyrd records |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Declare | A Service declaration: its components and the Verifiers bound to check them | Versioned Cards in the registry |
| Observe | Your service's behavior: verification results and drift observations, telemetry, and custom data | Rows in Bifrost, the Wyrd data plane |
| Verify | Nothing extra for triggered checks; the declaration says what is checked, when, and what happens on failure. Real-time checks are one call from your code | A verdict tied to the exact versions that ran, plus any failure actions the declaration names |

**Declare.** You declare a whole service in YAML, independent of the language it is written in. The declaration is a set of Cards. A Card is a versioned declaration of one part of your system, or of how that part is checked. See [Cards, versions, and relationships](/wyrd/understand/cards-versions-and-relationships/).

**Observe.** Observe is how you record what the declared system actually does. Observations go straight into Bifrost, the Wyrd data plane. See [Runs, observations, and retained evidence](/wyrd/understand/runs-observations-and-evidence/).

**Verify.** A Verifier judges observed behavior against a standard. Wyrd runs it for you when its Trigger fires, on a schedule or as observations arrive, and stores the verdict; a failed verdict runs the binding's Operators. Your code can also call a Verifier directly while a request is in flight and act on the answer. See [How verification works](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/).

## Where Wyrd stops

Wyrd judges your AI system; it does not run it. Your model, agent, or HTTP service keeps running in your own runtime and calls Wyrd to record what it did. Wyrd is not an application runtime, training framework, workflow engine, or general-purpose code executor.

| Your runtime owns | The Wyrd server owns |
| --- | --- |
| Your application code | Cards and their versions |
| Running and deploying the service | Observations and the queries over them |
| The service's Wyrd API key, kept in your secret store | Verdicts, failure actions, policy decisions, and the audit log |

Your service calls Wyrd as itself. Declaring a Service or Agent gives it a principal: an identity in your tenant with its own permissions. It may record observations only about the Cards in its own declaration, and every observation and verdict names the principal that produced it. See [Identity and authorization](/wyrd/understand/identity-and-authorization/).

The SDKs, the CLI, MCP, and HTTP all call the same server, so a verdict reads the same from Python, from Rust, or from an agent over MCP.

The one exception to this split is the AI Gateway, an optional proxy for your model and provider calls that also manages provider credentials and usage. If you route calls through it, Wyrd sits in your runtime's call path and records every call itself, not only the observations your code sends.

# Set up Wyrd

Page: /wyrd/get-started/setup/

> Run a Wyrd server on your machine, save its first credential, and make an authenticated request.

`wyrd server dev` starts a local Wyrd server, creates a tenant, optionally configures the LLM gateway from provider keys in your environment, and saves everything so every CLI and SDK process on your machine can call it. You supply PostgreSQL; the command does the rest.

## Prerequisites

- macOS on Apple silicon, or glibc Linux on x86_64 or arm64.
- The `wyrd` CLI, which ships in the Python and TypeScript packages:

  ```bash
  pip install wyrd-ai          # or: npm install -g wyrd-ai
  ```

- PostgreSQL 16 with an ordinary login that owns the `wyrd` database. The server refuses superuser and `BYPASSRLS` logins.

With Docker, this gives you a suitable database. The image's `postgres` user is a superuser, so the commands create a separate `wyrd` login:

```bash
docker run -d --name wyrd-postgres -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres -p 5432:5432 postgres:16
docker exec -i wyrd-postgres psql -U postgres <<'SQL'
CREATE ROLE wyrd LOGIN PASSWORD 'wyrd';
CREATE DATABASE wyrd OWNER wyrd;
SQL
```

## Start local Wyrd

`wyrd server dev` runs in the foreground and serves until you stop it. Run it in a terminal you keep open, or as a background job you own. It is a development server: a team or production deployment runs the standalone `wyrd-server` from its container image on a platform that manages its lifetime, as in [Deploy Wyrd for a team](/wyrd/operate/deploy-wyrd-for-a-team/).

```bash
wyrd server dev
```

When a coding agent does the work, you start the server and the agent connects to it once it is ready, through MCP and the saved CLI and SDK settings. The agent does not start, stop, or restart it.

On a terminal, the command asks for what it cannot find: the PostgreSQL URL (typed with echo off, for example `postgresql://wyrd:wyrd@127.0.0.1:5432/wyrd`) and the tenant slug, such as `acme`. Each input is taken from, in order, a command argument, its environment variable, the saved setting, and finally that question:

| Input | Argument | Environment | Saved in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Database | none: never an argument | `WYRD_DATABASE_URL`, optional `WYRD_PLATFORM_DATABASE_URL` | `credentials.toml` `[dev]` |
| Tenant | `--tenant` | none | `config.toml` `[dev].tenant` |
| HTTP listener | `--bind` | `WYRD_SERVER_BIND` | `config.toml` `[dev].bind` |
| gRPC listener | `--grpc-bind` | `WYRD_GRPC_BIND` | `config.toml` `[dev].grpc_bind` |
| Object storage | `--storage-url` (no credentials) | `WYRD_STORAGE_URL` | `config.toml` `[dev].storage_url` |
| Bifrost data | none | `WYRD_BIFROST_DATA_DIR` | `config.toml` `[dev].bifrost_data_dir` |

Listeners default to `127.0.0.1:8080` (HTTP) and `127.0.0.1:50051` (gRPC) and must be loopback. Without `WYRD_STORAGE_URL`, the command says so and uses `server/data/storage` and `server/data/bifrost` under the config directory, saved as absolute paths, so the working directory no longer matters. An existing `./.wyrd` directory is never adopted silently; to keep using it, pass `--storage-url file:///abs/path/.wyrd/storage` and set `WYRD_BIFROST_DATA_DIR`.

Scripts and agents pass everything up front and add `--non-interactive`. A run without a terminal, or with that flag, never asks; it lists every missing input together and exits before downloading, migrating, or creating anything:

```bash
export WYRD_DATABASE_URL="postgresql://wyrd:wyrd@127.0.0.1:5432/wyrd"
wyrd server dev --tenant acme --non-interactive
```

For a background job a script can wait on, add `--format json`. The command still serves in the foreground of that job. Once the server is ready it prints exactly one line to stdout, the readiness result, and keeps serving; progress and the server's own output go to the log file the result names, not to either stream:

```bash
wyrd server dev --tenant acme --non-interactive --format json > ready.json 2> error.json &
until [ -s ready.json ] || [ -s error.json ]; do sleep 1; done
cat ready.json error.json
```

```json
{"ready":true,"endpoint":"http://127.0.0.1:8080","grpc":"http://127.0.0.1:50051","tenant":"acme","storage_url":"file:///home/you/.config/wyrd/server/data/storage","bifrost_data_dir":"/home/you/.config/wyrd/server/data/bifrost","config_dir":"/home/you/.config/wyrd","gateway":"skipped; configure it later with wyrd gateway deployment put --file","mcp":null,"log":"/home/you/.config/wyrd/server/logs/server-dev.log"}
```

`storage_url` never carries credentials, and `mcp` is `null` unless you passed `--host`. A failure, before readiness or after it, writes one error document to stderr instead, with its stable `code`, `remediation`, and `details.stage`, and the command exits nonzero. Stop the job with `kill -INT` or by ending the terminal that owns it.

The first run downloads the newest server release, migrates the database, starts the server, saves its settings, and creates the tenant. It ends with a summary:

```text
Local Wyrd ready at http://127.0.0.1:8080 for tenant acme.
  gRPC: http://127.0.0.1:50051
  Storage: file:///home/you/.config/wyrd/server/data/storage
  Bifrost data: /home/you/.config/wyrd/server/data/bifrost
  Saved settings: /home/you/.config/wyrd/config.toml ([client], [dev]); key and database URLs: /home/you/.config/wyrd/credentials.toml
  Gateway: skipped; configure it later with wyrd gateway deployment put --file
Fresh SDK and CLI processes use these saved settings without exporting a key or endpoint. Press Ctrl-C to stop.
```

The first run also creates the platform root, whose credential administers tenants. It is printed once, to your terminal only, never to stdout or stderr. Store it somewhere safe: it is how you recover a lost tenant credential.

### Optional: the LLM gateway

A first interactive run offers the provider keys it finds in the environment: `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY` (else `GEMINI_API_KEY`), and `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` for Jev. It shows only provider, variable, and proposed deployment name, never a value. Pick any subset, rename the deployments, and confirm; the server seals the keys and creates the credentials and deployments in one transaction. Declining, or having no keys, still ends ready. No provider is called, so the summary does not claim a key works.

Unattended runs skip the offer. To configure the gateway without questions, pass a document whose credentials name environment variables, such as [`examples/gateway-setup/gateway.json`](https://github.com/bohmian-ai/wyrd/tree/main/examples/gateway-setup); `--gateway-file` applies it on every run that passes it, restarts included. `--skip-gateway` skips the offer explicitly. See [Set up the LLM gateway](/wyrd/connect/set-up-the-llm-gateway/).

Interactive runs then offer to connect the coding agents they find, such as Claude Code or Codex, through MCP. Accept, or skip and connect a host later. Without a terminal, name the host; the command never writes a credential into the host's configuration, and rerunning it changes nothing that is already in place:

```bash
wyrd mcp install --host claude-code --format json
```

Restart or reconnect the host afterwards so it loads the Wyrd server. A new agent then calls `wyrd.guide` with `{"topic":"start"}`, as the server's instructions tell it to. [Connect an agent through MCP](/wyrd/connect/connect-an-agent-through-mcp/) lists every host.

What the command saved, in your Wyrd config directory (`WYRD_CONFIG_HOME`, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/wyrd`, else `~/.config/wyrd`):

| File | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `credentials.toml` | The tenant administrator's API key, as `[default].api_key`, and the database URLs, as `[dev]`, readable only by you |
| `config.toml` | The HTTP and gRPC endpoints, as `[client].http_url` and `[client].grpc_url`, and the non-secret `[dev]` settings above |
| `server/sealing.key` | The key that encrypts stored secrets such as gateway provider keys, readable only by you |
| `server/data/` | Local object storage and Bifrost data, unless you chose other locations |

## Check it works

Keep the server running. In a second terminal:

```bash
wyrd list
```

A new tenant has no Cards, so the list is empty and the command exits 0. You exported no key or URL; the CLI read both from the saved config.

The SDKs read the same config, so code needs no URL or key either:

**Python**

```python
from wyrd.bifrost import Bifrost

bifrost = Bifrost.connect()
print([table["name"] for table in bifrost.list_tables()])
```

**Rust**

```rust
use wyrd_ai::{Bifrost, bifrost::BifrostOptions};

let bifrost = Bifrost::connect(BifrostOptions::default()).await?;
for table in bifrost.list_tables().await? {
    println!("{}.{}", table.namespace, table.name);
}
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { Bifrost } from "wyrd-ai";

const bifrost = await Bifrost.connect();
console.log((await bifrost.listTables()).map((table) => table.name));
```

Even a new tenant lists Wyrd's built-in tables. `connect` checks the credential before it returns, so a missing or refused key fails here, not on your first real call.

## Stop and restart

Press Ctrl-C in the server terminal. To restart, from any directory, with nothing exported:

```bash
wyrd server dev
```

The restart reuses the saved database, listeners, tenant, data paths, key, and sealing key, and asks nothing. Migrations are safe to rerun, and an existing tenant keeps its key; the command never issues a replacement just because it restarted. An argument or environment variable overrides only its own saved setting. A different `--tenant` while a key is saved is refused, as is a database whose server does not accept the saved key (a saved `wyrd auth login` never stands in for it), a saved key that local setup did not create, or a config directory that already selects another Wyrd server; use a separate `WYRD_CONFIG_HOME` for another tenant or deployment. Changing only a listener, such as `--bind`, resumes the same deployment without repeating the gateway or MCP host offers.

Your data lives in two places; keep both: the PostgreSQL database and the config directory. Lose `server/sealing.key` and stored provider keys can no longer be decrypted, so you would put them again. A key you supply through `WYRD_SEALING_KEY_FILE` or `WYRD_SEALING_KEY_BASE64` on the first run is kept there, so later runs need no variable; a different key on a later run is refused rather than replacing it.

## If it fails

| You see | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WYRD_CLI_503_SERVER_DEV` naming the `input` stage | An input is missing or invalid | Set the named variable or argument, or run on a terminal to be asked |
| `WYRD_CLI_503_SERVER_DEV` naming the `migration` stage | The database is unreachable, or the login does not own it | Check `WYRD_DATABASE_URL` and the `OWNER` of the `wyrd` database, then rerun |
| `WYRD_CLI_503_SERVER_DEV` naming the `listener` stage | Port 8080 is taken | Set `WYRD_SERVER_BIND` to a free loopback address and rerun |
| `is a superuser` or `BYPASSRLS` | `WYRD_DATABASE_URL` names an administrator login | Use the `wyrd` login created above |
| `WYRD_CLI_503_SERVER_DEV` naming the `local persistence` stage | The config directory is not writable | Restore its permissions and rerun; no tenant key was issued |
| `WYRD_CLI_503_SERVER_DEV` naming the `saved credential` stage after the tenant is active | The one-time tenant key was lost | Rerun on a terminal with `WYRD_PLATFORM_CREDENTIAL` set to the platform root and confirm rotation, or run `wyrd platform tenant recover-admin` |
| A gateway problem after the server is ready | Gateway setup did not complete; tenant setup remains. A refused document applies nothing, but if the response was lost the changes may have committed | Inspect with `wyrd gateway deployment list`, correct the document or keys, and rerun; reapplying the same named document is safe. Or pass `--skip-gateway` |
| `WYRD_CLI_400_SERVER_HOST_UNSUPPORTED` | No server release exists for this machine | Use a supported host from the prerequisites |
| `WYRD_CLIENT_401_NO_CREDENTIALS` from `wyrd list` or `connect` | No saved credential is visible to this process | Use the same `WYRD_CONFIG_HOME` as the server terminal |
| Calls go to the wrong server, or a key is refused | `WYRD_API_KEY`, `WYRD_ACCESS_TOKEN`, or `WYRD_SERVER_URL` is exported from other work, and it wins over the saved config | Unset them |

A failed run stops the server. Migrations and tenant creation that already committed stay, so rerunning the same command picks up where it stopped.

## Next

[Verify your first agent](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/): run a support agent against this server and get verdicts on its answers.

# Verify your first agent

Page: /wyrd/get-started/quickstart/

> Run the support-desk API against your local server, get verdicts from three Verifiers, and query the evidence behind them.

You will run `support-desk`, a small customer-support API, against the local server from [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/). Each question it answers is one Wyrd Run, and three Verifiers judge the answer:

| Verifier | Bound to | Checks | How it runs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `no-refund-promise` | The Service | The answer never contains `guaranteed refund` | Your code calls it and waits; no model |
| `ticket-complete` | The agent | The ticket has an answer and an order ID | Your code calls it and waits; sandboxed Python, no model |
| `follows-policy` | The agent | A refund decision letter the agent writes follows the refund policy | Your code queues it; the server runs a model judge in the background |

At the end you have a verdict for every check, each tied to the exact Card versions that ran, and one SQL query that joins it to the ticket, the trace, and the model call.

The code is the same app in Python, Rust, and TypeScript. This page runs the Python one; the tabs show the matching Rust and TypeScript code.

## Prerequisites

- A local server running from [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/), in another terminal. The app reads the endpoint and credential that setup saved, so you export nothing.
- An OpenAI API key with access to `gpt-4o` (the agent) and `gpt-6-luna` (the policy judge).
- Python 3.11+ and `git`.

## 1. Get the example

```bash
git clone https://github.com/bohmian-ai/wyrd.git
cd wyrd/examples/support-desk-app/python
pip install "wyrd-ai[agents,gateway,otel]" fastapi uvicorn
```

The `agents` extra brings the OpenAI Agents SDK, `gateway` the HTTP client the gateway uses, and `otel` the trace exporter. The Cards the app runs live next door, in `examples/support-desk-app/service/`.

## 2. Connect the model

Wyrd calls OpenAI for you, so your code never holds the OpenAI key. If you accepted the OpenAI key during setup, with the proposed deployment name `openai`, this step is already done.

Otherwise, with `OPENAI_API_KEY` exported, apply one document. It names the variable instead of holding the key; the CLI reads the value and sends it once, and the server encrypts it, so no read ever returns it:

```bash
wyrd gateway deployment put --file - <<'JSON'
{
  "credentials": [{"name": "openai-key", "provider": "openai", "source": {"local_env": "OPENAI_API_KEY"}}],
  "deployments": [{"name": "openai", "adapter": "openai", "auth": {"bearer": {"credential": "openai-key"}}}]
}
JSON
```

The server creates the **credential** `openai-key` and the **deployment** `openai` together, or neither, and prints both with the secret redacted. Agents now reach OpenAI models as `openai/<model>`, and both Agent Cards in the example ask for exactly that with `execution_route: {kind: wyrd_gateway, deployment: openai}`. [Set up the LLM gateway](/wyrd/connect/set-up-the-llm-gateway/) covers other providers and the separate credential and deployment commands.

## 3. Read what is declared

The example is seven Cards in `service/`. The Service names the others by relative path, such as `ref: ./support-agent.yaml`, so switch tabs to follow each reference:

**support-desk.yaml**

```yaml title="service/support-desk.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: support-desk
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  service_type: agent
  # The Service's own Verifier checks every answer the desk gives.
  verified_by:
    - verifier: ./no-refund-promise.yaml
  tables:
    - name: tickets
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          question: {type: string}
          answer: {type: string}
        required: [question, answer]
  components:
    - alias: agent
      ref: ./support-agent.yaml
      verified_by:
        - verifier: ./ticket-complete.yaml
        - verifier: ./follows-policy.yaml
    - alias: prompt
      ref: ./support-prompt.yaml

```

**support-agent.yaml**

```yaml title="service/support-agent.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: support-agent
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  prompt: ./support-prompt.yaml
  execution_route:
    kind: wyrd_gateway
    deployment: openai
  tool_names: []
  run_config:
    max_iterations: 1

```

**support-prompt.yaml**

```yaml title="service/support-prompt.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Prompt
metadata:
  name: support-prompt
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  provider: openai
  model: gpt-4o
  messages:
  - role: user
    content: 'Answer the customer: {{question}}'

```

**no-refund-promise.yaml**

```yaml title="service/no-refund-promise.yaml"
# The Service-wide check: whatever component answers, the desk never promises
# a guaranteed refund. One assertion, no model.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: no-refund-promise
  version: 1.0.0
  space: support
spec:
  description: A support answer never promises a guaranteed refund.
  inputs:
    answer: {type: json}
  requirements:
    - id: no-refund-promise
      statement: The answer never promises a guaranteed refund
      check: {kind: assert, path: inputs.answer, operator: not_contains, expected: guaranteed refund}

```

**ticket-complete.yaml**

```yaml title="service/ticket-complete.yaml"
# A code check: sandboxed Python reads the ticket and names every field the
# help desk needs that is missing. No model.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: ticket-complete
  version: 1.0.0
  space: support
spec:
  description: A support ticket carries the fields the help desk needs.
  inputs:
    ticket: {type: json}
  requirements:
    - id: ticket-complete
      statement: The ticket has an answer and an order id
      check:
        kind: code
        entrypoint: check
        inputs: {ticket: inputs.ticket}
        source:
          inline: |
            def check(ticket):
                missing = [field for field in ("answer", "order_id") if not ticket.get(field)]
                return {
                    "outcome": "failed" if missing else "passed",
                    "reason": "missing " + ", ".join(missing) if missing else "all fields present",
                    "citations": [{"slot": "ticket", "locator": {"json_pointer": ""}}],
                }

```

**follows-policy.yaml**

```yaml title="service/follows-policy.yaml"
# The support agent writes a refund decision letter; this Verifier checks the
# letter against the refund policy. The policy is fixed in policy-judge's
# prompt, so the letter is the only evidence the app sends, and a new policy
# means a new judge and Verifier version. The judge calls a model, so the app
# runs this one in the background.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: follows-policy
  version: 1.0.0
  space: support
spec:
  description: A refund decision letter follows the refund policy.
  inputs:
    letter: {type: media, formats: [markdown], max_bytes: 1048576}
  steps:
    # Turn the uploaded file into text the judge can read and cite by line.
    - id: read-letter
      action: {kind: extract, from: inputs.letter}
  requirements:
    - id: follows-policy
      statement: The letter's refund decision follows the refund policy
      check:
        kind: agent
        agent: ./policy-judge.yaml
        inputs:
          claim: requirement.statement
          letter: steps.read-letter.output

```

**policy-judge.yaml**

```yaml title="service/policy-judge.yaml"
# A tool-less judge. The refund policy lives in its prompt, so every verdict
# names the exact policy it applied. It returns a Verdict that cites the
# lines of the letter it relied on.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: policy-judge
  version: 1.0.0
  space: support
spec:
  execution_route: {kind: wyrd_gateway, deployment: openai}
  run_config: {max_iterations: 1}
  prompt:
    provider: openai
    model: gpt-6-luna
    system: |
      You check refund decision letters against this refund policy:
      1. Refunds of up to 100 dollars are approved within 30 days of purchase.
      2. Larger refunds need a manager's approval.
      Cite the lines of the letter your judgment rests on.
    messages:
      - role: user
        content: "Claim: {{claim}}. Letter: {{letter}}"
    response_format:
      type: object
      properties:
        outcome: {type: string, enum: [passed, failed, inconclusive]}
        reason: {type: string}
        citations:
          type: array
          items:
            type: object
            properties:
              slot: {type: string}
              locator:
                type: object
                properties:
                  lines:
                    type: object
                    properties:
                      start: {type: integer}
                      end: {type: integer}
                    required: [start, end]
                    additionalProperties: false
                required: [lines]
                additionalProperties: false
            required: [slot, locator]
            additionalProperties: false
      required: [outcome, reason, citations]
      additionalProperties: false

```

| Card | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `support-desk.yaml` | The Service: its components, its `tickets` table, and which Verifier checks what |
| `support-agent.yaml` | The agent. It runs `support-prompt` through the gateway's `openai` deployment |
| `support-prompt.yaml` | The prompt and model the agent runs |
| `no-refund-promise.yaml` | Bound to the Service. One assertion, no model |
| `ticket-complete.yaml` | Bound to the agent. A sandboxed Python check, no model |
| `follows-policy.yaml` | Bound to the agent. Extracts the text of the agent's letter, then asks `policy-judge` |
| `policy-judge.yaml` | A tool-less Agent with the refund policy in its prompt. Returns a verdict citing lines of the letter |

`verified_by` on the Service binds `no-refund-promise` to every Run of the Service. `verified_by` on the `agent` component binds the other two to the agent alone. Declaring the Service declares every Card it references, so the next step declares all seven.

## 4. Deploy the Cards

Check the declaration first. It validates all seven Cards and contacts no server:

```bash
wyrd declare ../service --check --format json
```

Then deploy:

```bash
python deploy.py
```

This declares all seven Cards, which creates the `vala.datasets.tickets` table. It then downloads the registered versions into `.wyrd-bundle/`, so the app runs exactly what the server holds, and turns on gateway metadata capture, so each model call is recorded with its Run:

**Python**

```python title="deploy.py"
cards = Cards(client)
receipt = cards.declare_from_path(SERVICE / "support-desk.yaml")
cards.pull(receipt.root, BUNDLE)
Gateway(client).put_capture_policy({"mode": "metadata", "payload_fields": []})
print(f"declared {receipt.root} into {BUNDLE.name}")
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let cards = Cards::connect_with(client).await?;
let receipt = cards
    .declare_from_path(service_dir().join("support-desk.yaml"))
    .await?;
cards
    .pull(
        CardSelector::exact(receipt.root),
        bundle,
        BundleMode::Complete,
    )
    .await?;
Gateway::connect_with(client)
    .await?
    .put_capture_policy(&GatewayCapturePolicyWrite {
        mode: GatewayCaptureMode::Metadata,
        payload_fields: BTreeSet::new(),
    })
    .await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="deploy.ts"
const cards = await Cards.connect({ client });
const receipt = await cards.declareFromPath(join(SERVICE_DIR, "support-desk.yaml"));
await cards.pull(receipt.root, bundle);
// Record each gateway call's metadata, never its content, in vala.gateway.calls.
await (await Gateway.connect({ client })).putCapturePolicy({ mode: "metadata", payload_fields: [] });
```

It ends with `declared <card-uid> into .wyrd-bundle`. Declaring is idempotent: running it again with unchanged Cards changes nothing. Declaring needs the `editor` role; a `viewer` credential is refused with `WYRD_PERMISSION_403_DENIED_RBAC`.

## 5. Start the app

The app connects once at startup. `WyrdState.from_path` loads the pulled bundle, `start_bifrost` starts the buffered writer for the `tickets` table, and telemetry exports spans, including the Agents SDK's own traces, to Wyrd:

**Python**

```python title="desk.py"
self.client = client or WyrdClient()
self.state = WyrdState.from_path(BUNDLE, self.client)
self.state.start_bifrost()
# Spans export to Wyrd through the SDK's OTLP exporter; the Agents SDK's
# own traces become spans too, under the request's Run.
self.state.start_telemetry()
set_trace_processors([WyrdAgentsTraceProcessor()])
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let state = WyrdState::from_path_with(bundle, client.clone())?;
// Starts the buffered writer the ticket rows go through.
state.start_bifrost().await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="server.ts"
// WYRD_SERVER_URL and WYRD_API_KEY, else the settings `wyrd server dev` saved, say which server to use and who the app is.
const client = WyrdClient.connect();
// The declared Service, pulled by `npm run deploy`.
const state = WyrdState.fromPath(BUNDLE_DIR, { client });
await state.startBifrost(); // writes tickets to Bifrost
await state.startTelemetry(); // exports spans to Wyrd
```

Rows and spans are buffered, so they reach Wyrd in batches, not on every call. On exit the app flushes them. In Python and TypeScript, `state.shutdown()` flushes the spans of the provider `start_telemetry` installed, then drains the writer. In Rust, `start_telemetry(&state)` returns a `Telemetry` handle that the server keeps while it serves; it flushes that handle before draining the state:

**Python**

```python title="app.py"
app.state.desk = Desk()
yield
# Flush buffered tickets and spans to Wyrd before exiting.
app.state.desk.state.shutdown()
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let telemetry = start_telemetry(&self.state)?;
let state = self.state.clone();
let served = axum::serve(listener, self.router())
    .with_graceful_shutdown(stop)
    .await;
// Flush spans first, then drain buffered tickets, before exiting.
telemetry.shutdown()?;
state.shutdown().await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="server.ts"
// Flush every span and row before exiting: shutdown flushes the provider startTelemetry installed, then drains the writer.
for (const signal of ["SIGINT", "SIGTERM"]) {
  process.on(signal, async () => {
    server.close();
    await state.shutdown();
    process.exit(0);
  });
}
```

A process killed before `shutdown()` loses whatever was still buffered.

Start the API, and leave it running:

```bash
uvicorn app:app
```

## 6. Ask a question

In another terminal, ask a question:

```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/ask -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"question": "Where is my order?", "order_id": "A-1001"}'
```

The handler answers in a new Run, records the ticket under it, then asks for both model-free verdicts and waits for them:

**Python**

```python title="desk.py"
run = self.state.run()
with run, tracer.start_as_current_span("support-desk.ask"):
    # These headers tie the gateway's record of the call to this Run.
    headers = {
        "wyrd-run-id": run.run_id,
        "wyrd-card-uid": str(self.state.card_ref("agent").uid),
    }
    model = OpenAIChatCompletionsModel(
        self.model, self.gateway.with_options(default_headers=headers)
    )
    agent = Agent(name="support-agent", model=model)
    result = await Runner.run(agent, self.template.replace("{{question}}", question))
    answer = str(result.final_output)
    run.observe.record(TICKETS, {"question": question, "answer": answer})
```

```python title="desk.py"
return {
    "no-refund-promise": run.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", answer=ticket["answer"]),
    "ticket-complete": run.for_card("agent").observe.verify(
        "ticket-complete", ticket=ticket
    ),
}
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let agent = self.state.agent(run.alias())?;
let ExecutionRoute::WyrdGateway { deployment } = &agent.card().spec.execution_route else {
    return Err(ApiError::internal(
        "the Agent does not route through the Wyrd gateway",
    ));
};
let prompt = &agent.prompt().metadata.prompt;
let rendered = prompt
    .render(&[("question", question)])
    .map_err(|_| ApiError::internal("the Agent's Prompt does not render"))?;
let mut body = serde_json::to_value(rendered)
    .map_err(|_| ApiError::internal("the rendered Prompt does not serialize"))?["body"]
    .take();
body["model"] = json!(format!("{deployment}/{}", prompt.model));
let client = self.state.client()?;
// These headers tie the gateway's record of the call to this Run.
let reply = reqwest::Client::new()
    .post(format!("{}/v1/chat/completions", client.server_url()))
    .bearer_auth(client.access_token().await?.expose())
    .header("wyrd-run-id", run.run_id().as_str())
    .header("wyrd-card-uid", run.subject_uid().as_str())
    .json(&body)
    .timeout(ANSWER_TIMEOUT)
    .send()
    .await
    .map_err(|_| ApiError::internal("the Wyrd gateway call failed"))?;
let status = reply.status();
let reply: Option<Value> = reply.json().await.ok();
if !status.is_success() {
    return Err(ApiError::refusal(status, reply.as_ref()));
}
let reply =
    reply.ok_or_else(|| ApiError::internal("the gateway reply could not be read"))?;
let answer = reply["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
    .as_str()
    .ok_or_else(|| ApiError::internal("the gateway reply carries no text"))?
    .to_owned();
run.observe()
    .record(
        "vala.datasets.tickets",
        &json!({ "question": question, "answer": answer }),
    )
    .await?;
```

```rust title="lib.rs"
let run = desk.state.run();
let agent = run.for_card("agent")?;
let work = async {
    let answer = desk.answer(&agent, &body.question).await?;
    let promise = run
        .observe()
        .verify(
            "no-refund-promise",
            Inputs::named([("answer", Input::from(json!(answer)))]),
        )
        .await?;
    let ticket = json!({
        "question": body.question,
        "answer": answer,
        "order_id": body.order_id,
    });
    let complete = agent
        .observe()
        .verify(
            "ticket-complete",
            Inputs::named([("ticket", Input::from(ticket))]),
        )
        .await?;
    Ok::<_, ApiError>((answer, promise, complete))
};
let (answer, promise, complete) = run
    .scope(work.instrument(tracing::info_span!("support-desk.ask")))
    .await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="server.ts"
const wyrdRun = support.state.run();
// Spans started inside the scope carry the Run's ID.
return wyrdRun.scope(async () => {
  const text = await answer(support.gateway, support.state, wyrdRun, question);
  await wyrdRun.observe.record(TICKETS, { question, answer: text });
  return check(wyrdRun, text);
});
```

```typescript title="server.ts"
const ticket = { question, answer: text, order_id: orderId ?? null };
const [promise, complete] = await Promise.all([
  wyrdRun.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", { answer: text }),
  wyrdRun.forCard("agent").observe.verify("ticket-complete", { ticket }),
]);
```

`run.observe.verify` checks against the Service's Verifiers; `run.for_card("agent").observe.verify` checks against the agent's. Both carry the same `run_id`.

Both calls are synchronous: `verify` returns once the verdict exists. The reply holds the Run ID, the answer, and each Verifier's verdict with one entry per requirement. This reply was captured from the Python SDK's integration run of this app, trimmed of each requirement's `check` and `provenance`; there a local model fixture wrote the answer, so your answer text will differ:

```json
{
  "run_id": "01a1512a-1238-7ea5-b9bb-a4f0ad0dab64",
  "answer": "Your order A-1001 ships tomorrow.",
  "checks": {
    "no-refund-promise": {
      "verdict": "passed",
      "requirements": [{
        "id": "no-refund-promise",
        "statement": "The answer never promises a guaranteed refund",
        "outcome": "passed",
        "reason": "the comparison held",
        "actual": "Your order A-1001 ships tomorrow."
      }]
    },
    "ticket-complete": {
      "verdict": "passed",
      "requirements": [{
        "id": "ticket-complete",
        "statement": "The ticket has an answer and an order id",
        "outcome": "passed",
        "reason": "all fields present",
        "citations": [{"slot": "ticket", "locator": {"json_pointer": ""}}]
      }]
    }
  }
}
```

Now drop the order ID and ask again:

```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/ask -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"question": "Where is my order?"}'
```

`ticket-complete` fails with the reason `missing order_id`. That is a verdict, not an error: the request succeeds, and your code decides what to do with a failed check. Keep the `run_id` from either reply for step 8.

A verify call that names a Verifier not bound to the Run's Card fails with `WYRD_SDK_404_UNKNOWN_VERIFIER`; evidence for a slot the Verifier doesn't declare fails with `WYRD_VERIFICATION_400_INPUT_INVALID`. Those are errors, not verdicts.

## 7. Queue a policy review

Some answers are documents. `POST /reviews` asks the agent to write a refund decision letter in Markdown, uploads the letter as the evidence for `follows-policy`, and replies at once with an execution ID. The judge calls a model, so the customer doesn't wait for it. `submit` only queues the check: a returned execution ID means the work is staged, not that a verdict exists:

```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/reviews -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"question": "Can I get a refund on a damaged item?"}'
```

**Python**

```python title="desk.py"
execution = run.for_card("agent").observe.submit(
    "follows-policy", letter=verify.File(letter.encode(), filename="letter.md")
)
assert isinstance(execution, verify.Execution)  # Run evidence always queues one
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let submission = run
    .observe()
    .submit("follows-policy", letter_inputs(&letter))
    .await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="server.ts"
const letter = verify.File.bytes(new TextEncoder().encode(text), { filename: "letter.md" });
const inputs = { letter };
const submitted = await wyrdRun.forCard("agent").observe.submit("follows-policy", inputs);
if (submitted.kind !== "queued") throw new Error("follows-policy judges Run evidence, so submit queues it");
```

The server runs it: an `extract` step turns the letter into text, then the tool-less `policy-judge` Agent, whose prompt holds the refund policy, decides whether the letter follows it and cites the lines it relied on. The policy never travels with the request; changing it means a new judge version, so every verdict names the policy it applied. Read the result back by its ID:

```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/reviews/<execution-id>
```

**Python**

```python title="app.py"
# Any process can pick a check up from its execution ID alone.
state = verify.Execution.connect(execution_id, request.app.state.desk.client).status()
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let state = Execution::connect_with(id, desk.state.client()?)
    .await?
    .status()
    .await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="server.ts"
const execution = await verify.Execution.connect(executionId, { client: support.client });
const { status, error, result } = await execution.status();
```

The first read can arrive before the queued execution is visible, and answers `404`:

```json
{"code": "WYRD_VERIFICATION_404_EXECUTION_NOT_FOUND", "message": "no verification execution with this ID in the caller's tenant"}
```

Read again. `status` then moves from `pending` to `running` to `completed`. A completed review, captured from the same integration run and trimmed of `check` and `provenance`:

```json
{
  "execution_id": "d4be3e01-88fd-7d99-a6e7-5fbf4b775bef",
  "status": "completed",
  "verdict": "passed",
  "requirements": [{
    "id": "follows-policy",
    "statement": "The letter's refund decision follows the refund policy",
    "outcome": "passed",
    "reason": "a 40 dollar refund within 30 days is approved",
    "citations": [{"slot": "letter", "locator": {"lines": {"start": 4, "end": 5}}}]
  }]
}
```

The citation points at lines 4 and 5 of the letter. Its `provenance` names the exact judge Agent, Prompt version, and gateway route that decided. `errored`, `timed_out`, and `cancelled` are terminal too: they carry an `error` with a stable code instead of a verdict, so stop polling on any of them. `retrying` means read again. [Run a verification and inspect its evidence](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/run-a-verification-and-inspect-its-evidence/) covers every status, and what to do if an execution stays not found.

Nothing about the ID is tied to the process that queued it. Any process with the credential can read it.

## 8. Query the evidence

Every piece of the Run landed in Bifrost, Wyrd's warehouse, keyed by the same `run_id`. One query joins the ticket, the request span, the gateway call, and every verdict:

```python title="evidence.py"
SQL = """
SELECT t.run_id, t.question, t.answer, s.trace_id, g.call_id, r.execution_id, r.verdict
FROM vala.datasets.tickets t
JOIN vala.traces.spans s ON s.run_id = t.run_id AND s.name = 'support-desk.ask'
JOIN vala.gateway.calls g ON g.run_id = t.run_id
JOIN vala.verification.results r ON r.run_id = t.run_id
WHERE t.run_id = $1
"""
```

```bash
python evidence.py <run-id>
```

It prints one row per gateway call and verdict for that Run. For the first `/ask` Run above, after the app had shut down and flushed, the integration run printed two rows, one per verdict:

```text
{'run_id': '01a1512a-1238-7ea5-b9bb-a4f0ad0dab64', 'question': 'Where is my order?', 'answer': 'Your order A-1001 ships tomorrow.', 'trace_id': b'e\xf8\xf7+AS7\x9b>=K\xca?|I\x08', 'call_id': '01a1512a-1322-7780-8ea1-475e61e2de0d', 'execution_id': '01a1512a-1348-7223-9310-e27a7b1f114e', 'verdict': 'passed'}
{'run_id': '01a1512a-1238-7ea5-b9bb-a4f0ad0dab64', 'question': 'Where is my order?', 'answer': 'Your order A-1001 ships tomorrow.', 'trace_id': b'e\xf8\xf7+AS7\x9b>=K\xca?|I\x08', 'call_id': '01a1512a-1322-7780-8ea1-475e61e2de0d', 'execution_id': '01a1512a-1341-7a51-ac0a-b2e5d3c5c3cc', 'verdict': 'passed'}
```

Evidence is not instant. Tickets and spans are buffered in the app, and verdicts are written in batches by the server, so a query right after a request can return fewer rows. Query again, or stop the app first so it flushes. The same SQL runs from the CLI with `wyrd query --sql`.

## If it fails

| You see | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A gateway error naming `openai/gpt-4o` or `openai/gpt-6-luna` | No `openai` deployment, or the key lacks that model | Run [step 2](#2-connect-the-model) and check the key's model access |
| `WYRD_CLIENT_401_NO_CREDENTIALS` | The app found no saved credential | Run it with the same `WYRD_CONFIG_HOME` as the server from setup |
| `WYRD_VALA_409_BIFROST_FINGERPRINT_MISMATCH` | A `vala.datasets.tickets` table with different columns already exists in this tenant | Use a fresh tenant in its own config directory, such as `WYRD_CONFIG_HOME=~/.config/wyrd-quickstart wyrd server dev --tenant quickstart` |
| The app can't find `.wyrd-bundle` | The Cards were never deployed | Run `python deploy.py` from the `python/` directory |
| A review stays `pending` | The server is not running background verification | Check the server terminal for errors |
| `WYRD_VERIFICATION_404_EXECUTION_NOT_FOUND` right after `/reviews` | The queued execution is not visible yet | Read it again |
| The evidence query returns no rows | Rows are still buffered in the app or the server | Query again, or stop the app so it flushes |
| `WYRD_CLI_409_SERVER_VERSION_INCOMPATIBLE` | The CLI and server are different minor versions | Use a CLI and server from the same release |

## Adapt it to your own app

The same three moves apply to any application you own:

1. **Declare.** Write a Service Card whose `components` pin each Agent, Prompt, or other part by exact version, whose `tables` hold the rows you record, and whose `verified_by` binds Verifiers. A hosted model your Prompt names, such as `openai/gpt-4o`, is not a Model Card; declare a `Model` Card only for a model artifact you own and version. Run `wyrd declare <dir> --check --format json`, then `wyrd declare <dir> --format json`, then `wyrd pull` the root into a bundle. [Define a Service](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/define-a-service/) covers each field.
2. **Observe.** Load the bundle with `WyrdState.from_path`, start Bifrost and telemetry once at startup, wrap each unit of work in `state.run()`, record rows with `run.observe.record`, and call `state.shutdown()` on exit. [Record a Run and observations](/wyrd/build-and-verify/observe/record-a-run-and-observations/) shows each call.
3. **Verify.** Call `verify` where your code must act on the verdict, and `submit` where it must not wait, then read the execution by ID until it is terminal. [Run a verification and inspect its evidence](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/run-a-verification-and-inspect-its-evidence/) covers both.

A coding agent connected through MCP can follow the same path: `wyrd.guide {"topic": "start"}` returns it step by step.

## Clean up

Stop the API with Ctrl-C, then remove the deployment and the stored key:

```bash
wyrd gateway deployment delete openai
wyrd gateway credential delete openai-key
```

Your Cards and verdicts stay in the database and `.wyrd/`. Delete those as described in [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/#stop-and-restart) to start over.

## Next

- [Set up the LLM gateway](/wyrd/connect/set-up-the-llm-gateway/): route other providers and see what each call records.
- The Rust and TypeScript tabs are reference copies, compiled against the public SDKs by this repository's `check:examples` and `ts:typecheck` lanes. The runnable apps, with manifests and tests, are in the `wyrd-example-py`, `wyrd-example-rs`, and [`wyrd-example-ts`](https://github.com/bohmian-ai/wyrd-example-ts) repositories.

# Define a Service

Page: /wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/define-a-service/

> Declare a Service as a folder of Card files, with exact component versions and a table for the rows it records, then validate it locally.

A Service Card is the root of your declaration. It names the components your service is built from, each pinned to an exact Card version, and the tables it records rows into. You write it in YAML whatever language the service is written in, and `wyrd declare --check` checks it without a server.

This page builds the `support-desk` Service from the [quickstart](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/). The finished files are in `examples/support-desk-app/service/`.

## 1. Write the components

Each component is its own Card file with an exact `metadata.version`. The support desk has an Agent and the Prompt it runs. The Agent points at the Prompt by relative path:

**support-agent.yaml**

```yaml title="support-agent.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: support-agent
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  prompt: ./support-prompt.yaml
  execution_route:
    kind: wyrd_gateway
    deployment: openai
  tool_names: []
  run_config:
    max_iterations: 1

```

**support-prompt.yaml**

```yaml title="support-prompt.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Prompt
metadata:
  name: support-prompt
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  provider: openai
  model: gpt-4o
  messages:
  - role: user
    content: 'Answer the customer: {{question}}'

```

`execution_route` says how the Agent reaches its model: `wyrd_gateway` sends it through the gateway deployment named `openai`, which [Set up the LLM gateway](/wyrd/connect/set-up-the-llm-gateway/) creates. Use `{kind: native}` when your own code calls the model.

The Prompt's `provider` and `model` name a hosted model, such as `openai` and `gpt-4o`, and the gateway resolves `openai/gpt-4o` at call time. That string is not a Model Card and needs none. Declare a `Model` Card only for a model artifact you own and version, such as a trained classifier or a fine-tune, so verdicts and drift attach to its exact version.

## 2. Write the Service

The Service gives each component an `alias`, the name your code uses at runtime, such as `state.run("agent")`:

```yaml title="support-desk.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: support-desk
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  service_type: agent
  tables:
    - name: tickets
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          question: {type: string}
          answer: {type: string}
        required: [question, answer]
  components:
    - alias: agent
      ref: ./support-agent.yaml
    - alias: prompt
      ref: ./support-prompt.yaml
```

| Field | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `components[].alias` | The runtime name of the component, unique within the Service |
| `components[].ref` | A path to the component's Card file, or a declared Card such as `{kind: Model, name: churn-classifier, version: 1.4.2}` |
| `tables[].name` | A table to create as `vala.datasets.<name>` when the Service registers |
| `tables[].schema` | A JSON Schema object; the order of `properties` is the column order |
| `service_type` | A free-form label, such as `agent` or `api` |

A path is relative to the file that contains it. Every reference names one exact version: Wyrd has no version ranges, so a declared Service always records exactly what it was built from.

Verifiers attach through `verified_by`, which [Bind a Verifier](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/bind-a-verifier/) adds next.

## 3. Check it locally

```bash
wyrd declare --check support-desk.yaml
```

`wyrd declare --check` loads the Service and every Card it references, validates them, and contacts no server. It prints `check valid: 3 card(s)`, then one line per Card, such as `Service default/support-desk@1.0.0`. Fix anything it reports before you declare.

## Set the space once

`space` groups related Cards, such as a team's. Instead of writing it in every file, put a `wyrd.toml` next to your Cards or in any parent directory:

```toml
[defaults]
space = "support"

[kind.Verifier]
space = "support-verifiers"
```

A Card's own `metadata.space` wins, then the `[kind.<Kind>]` value, then `[defaults]`, then `default`. `wyrd.toml` can also set `labels` and `annotations`, but never `name` or `version`.

## If it fails

| You see | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WYRD_LOADER_400_INVALID_ENVELOPE` | A file is missing `apiVersion` or `kind`, a path points at no Card, a referenced Card has no exact `version`, or two Cards reference each other. `details.diagnostics` names each file | Fix the file it names |
| `WYRD_LOADER_400_PATH_ESCAPE` | A `ref` path leaves the declaration's directory tree | Move the Card inside it, or reference the declared Card instead |

## Next

[Bind a Verifier](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/bind-a-verifier/) to say how the Service is checked.

# Bind a Verifier

Page: /wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/bind-a-verifier/

> Attach a Verifier to a Service or one of its components with verified_by, and choose whether your code or a schedule runs it.

A Verifier on its own checks nothing. You attach it to what it checks with a `verified_by` binding on the Service, on one component, or on an Agent Card. The binding also decides who runs it: your code, or a schedule.

## Bind a Verifier your code calls

This is the support desk's full Service. It binds one Verifier to the whole Service and two to the agent. Switch tabs to see each Card a binding points at:

**support-desk.yaml**

```yaml title="support-desk.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: support-desk
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  service_type: agent
  # The Service's own Verifier checks every answer the desk gives.
  verified_by:
    - verifier: ./no-refund-promise.yaml
  tables:
    - name: tickets
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          question: {type: string}
          answer: {type: string}
        required: [question, answer]
  components:
    - alias: agent
      ref: ./support-agent.yaml
      verified_by:
        - verifier: ./ticket-complete.yaml
        - verifier: ./follows-policy.yaml
    - alias: prompt
      ref: ./support-prompt.yaml

```

**no-refund-promise.yaml**

```yaml title="no-refund-promise.yaml"
# The Service-wide check: whatever component answers, the desk never promises
# a guaranteed refund. One assertion, no model.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: no-refund-promise
  version: 1.0.0
  space: support
spec:
  description: A support answer never promises a guaranteed refund.
  inputs:
    answer: {type: json}
  requirements:
    - id: no-refund-promise
      statement: The answer never promises a guaranteed refund
      check: {kind: assert, path: inputs.answer, operator: not_contains, expected: guaranteed refund}

```

**ticket-complete.yaml**

```yaml title="ticket-complete.yaml"
# A code check: sandboxed Python reads the ticket and names every field the
# help desk needs that is missing. No model.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: ticket-complete
  version: 1.0.0
  space: support
spec:
  description: A support ticket carries the fields the help desk needs.
  inputs:
    ticket: {type: json}
  requirements:
    - id: ticket-complete
      statement: The ticket has an answer and an order id
      check:
        kind: code
        entrypoint: check
        inputs: {ticket: inputs.ticket}
        source:
          inline: |
            def check(ticket):
                missing = [field for field in ("answer", "order_id") if not ticket.get(field)]
                return {
                    "outcome": "failed" if missing else "passed",
                    "reason": "missing " + ", ".join(missing) if missing else "all fields present",
                    "citations": [{"slot": "ticket", "locator": {"json_pointer": ""}}],
                }

```

**follows-policy.yaml**

```yaml title="follows-policy.yaml"
# The support agent writes a refund decision letter; this Verifier checks the
# letter against the refund policy. The policy is fixed in policy-judge's
# prompt, so the letter is the only evidence the app sends, and a new policy
# means a new judge and Verifier version. The judge calls a model, so the app
# runs this one in the background.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: follows-policy
  version: 1.0.0
  space: support
spec:
  description: A refund decision letter follows the refund policy.
  inputs:
    letter: {type: media, formats: [markdown], max_bytes: 1048576}
  steps:
    # Turn the uploaded file into text the judge can read and cite by line.
    - id: read-letter
      action: {kind: extract, from: inputs.letter}
  requirements:
    - id: follows-policy
      statement: The letter's refund decision follows the refund policy
      check:
        kind: agent
        agent: ./policy-judge.yaml
        inputs:
          claim: requirement.statement
          letter: steps.read-letter.output

```

**support-agent.yaml**

```yaml title="support-agent.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: support-agent
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  prompt: ./support-prompt.yaml
  execution_route:
    kind: wyrd_gateway
    deployment: openai
  tool_names: []
  run_config:
    max_iterations: 1

```

| Bound on | Verifier | Applies to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The Service's `verified_by` | `no-refund-promise` | Every Run of the Service, as `run.observe.verify(...)` |
| The `agent` component's `verified_by` | `ticket-complete`, `follows-policy` | The agent's view of a Run, as `run.for_card("agent").observe.verify(...)` |

None of these bindings has `runs_on`, so nothing runs them on its own. Your code calls `verify` or `submit` with the evidence; [Verify inside the run](/wyrd/build-and-verify/observe/record-a-run-and-observations/#3-record-verify-and-submit) shows both. That is the right default for anything that judges one request.

## Bind a Verifier to a schedule

A schedule judges samples your service recorded over time, such as request latency, instead of one request. Add `runs_on` with a Trigger and optionally `on_failure` with the Operators to run when it fails:

**latency-watch.yaml**

```yaml title="latency-watch.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: latency-watch
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  verified_by:
    - verifier: ./latency-shift.yaml
      runs_on: ./daily.yaml
      on_failure:
        - ./alert-on-call.yaml

```

**latency-shift.yaml**

```yaml title="latency-shift.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: latency-shift
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  description: Daily check that request latency has not shifted from the healthy baseline.
  inputs:
    latency: {type: samples, features: [latency]}
  requirements:
    - id: latency-unshifted
      statement: Request latency has not shifted from the healthy baseline
      check:
        kind: drift
        on: inputs.latency
        method: Psi
        signal:
          kind: Distribution
          baseline_ref: {kind: Data, name: latency-baseline, version: 1.0.0, space: default}
          features: [latency]
        condition: {kind: Statistical}
        profile:
          kind: Psi
          binning_strategy: {kind: EqualWidth, n_bins: 10}
          threshold: {kind: Fixed, value: 0.25}

```

**daily.yaml**

```yaml title="daily.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Trigger
metadata:
  name: daily
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  description: Once a day at midnight UTC.
  kind: schedule
  cron: "0 0 * * *"

```

**alert-on-call.yaml**

```yaml title="alert-on-call.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Operator
metadata:
  name: alert-on-call
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  description: Page the on-call hook when latency shifts. The origin comes from the connection.
  kind: http
  method: post
  url: /hooks/latency-shift
  auth:
    scheme: bearer
    connection: on-call-hooks
  body:
    execution_id: "{{execution_id}}"
    summary: "{{summary}}"

```

Every day at midnight UTC, the server compares the day's `latency` samples with the baseline and, on a `failed` verdict, posts to the on-call hook. [Monitor drift](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/monitor-drift/) walks through recording the samples.

## Binding fields

| Field | Required | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `verifier` | Yes | A path to the Verifier's Card file, or a declared Verifier |
| `runs_on` | No | A Trigger, as a path, a declared Card, or inline. Absent, only your code runs the Verifier |
| `on_failure` | No | Operators to run after a `failed` verdict, as paths, declared Cards, or inline |

A Trigger is `{kind: schedule, cron: "<cron>", tz: <zone>}`, with `tz` defaulting to UTC. Schedules only judge recorded samples: binding `runs_on` to a Verifier with other inputs fails declaration. A binding has no other fields, and an unknown field such as `when` is rejected.

## If it fails

| You see | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WYRD_SDK_404_UNKNOWN_VERIFIER` from `verify` or `submit` | The Verifier isn't bound to the view you called it on | Call it on the view whose Card binds it, or add the binding |
| `WYRD_SPEC_400_DUPLICATE_VERIFICATION_BINDING` | The same Verifier is bound twice on one subject | Remove one |
| `WYRD_SPEC_400_TRIGGER_ACTIVATION_MISMATCH` | `runs_on` is set on a Verifier that doesn't judge `samples` | Remove `runs_on` and call the Verifier from code |
| `WYRD_PERMISSION_403_DENIED_RBAC` at declaration | A binding has `on_failure`, and your credential lacks `operators:invoke` | Declare with a credential that has it |

## Next

[Declare and inspect the Service](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/declare-and-inspect/). To write your own Verifier, see [Author a Verifier](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/author-a-verifier/).

# Declare and inspect a Service

Page: /wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/declare-and-inspect/

> Declare a Service and every Card it references in one call, then read back its exact versions and the relationships the server derived.

Registering the Service registers every Card it references, dependencies first, and creates its tables. The server then records which Card references which, so you can read the graph back from any Card.

## Declare

From the CLI:

```bash
wyrd declare examples/support-desk-app/service/support-desk.yaml
```

It prints `declared:` and the Service's reference, then one line per Card with its outcome and status:

```text
declared: default/Service/support-desk@1.0.0#<uid>
  default/Prompt/support-prompt@1.0.0#<uid>: declared (active)
  ...
```

**Unverified:** The line format is derived from the CLI source. A captured run replaces it on the first verified run.

From code, `declare_from_path` does the same and returns the receipt. The example's deploy step then downloads what it declared:

**Python**

```python title="deploy.py"
cards = Cards(client)
receipt = cards.declare_from_path(SERVICE / "support-desk.yaml")
cards.pull(receipt.root, BUNDLE)
Gateway(client).put_capture_policy({"mode": "metadata", "payload_fields": []})
print(f"declared {receipt.root} into {BUNDLE.name}")
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let cards = Cards::connect_with(client).await?;
let receipt = cards
    .declare_from_path(service_dir().join("support-desk.yaml"))
    .await?;
cards
    .pull(
        CardSelector::exact(receipt.root),
        bundle,
        BundleMode::Complete,
    )
    .await?;
Gateway::connect_with(client)
    .await?
    .put_capture_policy(&GatewayCapturePolicyWrite {
        mode: GatewayCaptureMode::Metadata,
        payload_fields: BTreeSet::new(),
    })
    .await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="deploy.ts"
const cards = await Cards.connect({ client });
const receipt = await cards.declareFromPath(join(SERVICE_DIR, "support-desk.yaml"));
await cards.pull(receipt.root, bundle);
// Record each gateway call's metadata, never its content, in vala.gateway.calls.
await (await Gateway.connect({ client })).putCapturePolicy({ mode: "metadata", payload_fields: [] });
```

`receipt.root` is the Service's exact reference, and `receipt.outcomes` lists every Card with its outcome:

| Outcome | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `declared` | A new version was stored |
| `idempotent_noop` | That exact version is already declared with the same content |
| `deduplicated` | The Card has no exact version, and the latest one in its line has the same content |

Declaring is safe to rerun: unchanged Cards come back `idempotent_noop`. If the loader finds any error, nothing is sent.

## Inspect

List what is declared:

```bash
wyrd list --kind Service
```

Fetch one Card with the relationships the server derived. You never write `relationships`; the server reads every reference in each `spec` and records the edge both ways:

**Python**

```python
from wyrd.cards import CardRef, Cards

card = Cards().get(CardRef("Service", "support-desk", "1.0.0", space="default"))
for edge in card.relationships["outbound_refs"]:
    print(edge.get("alias"), edge["ref"])
```

**Rust**

```rust
use wyrd_ai::cards::{CardRef, CardSelector, Cards};

let service: CardRef = "default/Service/support-desk@1.0.0".parse()?;
let card = Cards::connect().await?.get(CardSelector::exact(service)).await?;
for edge in &card.relationships.outbound_refs {
    println!("{edge:?}");
}
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { Cards } from "wyrd-ai";

const card = await (await Cards.connect()).get("default/Service/support-desk@1.0.0");
for (const edge of card.relationships.outbound_refs) console.log(edge.alias, edge.ref);
```

`outbound_refs` lists every Card this one references, with the component `alias` where there is one. `inbound_refs` lists every Card that references it, so fetching `support-prompt` shows both the Agent and the Service that use it. `status.phase` is the Card's lifecycle state, such as `active`.

To download the Service and everything it references into a directory, as the app does at deploy time:

```bash
wyrd pull --kind Service --space default --name support-desk --version 1.0.0 --output-dir .wyrd-bundle
```

## Change a Card

An exact version is immutable. To change `support-prompt`, give it a new `version`, update the reference to it in `support-agent.yaml`, and bump the Agent and the Service the same way. Register again, and the new Service version records the new Prompt while the old one still names the old Prompt. That is what keeps an old verdict reproducible.

Leave `version` out of a Card instead, and the server picks one: `0.1.0` first, then the next patch whenever the content changes. That suits Cards you iterate on; we recommend exact versions for anything a Service pins.

## If it fails

| You see | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WYRD_REGISTRY_409_SPEC_DRIFT` | An exact version is already declared with different content | Bump the Card's `version` |
| `WYRD_REGISTRY_422_UNRESOLVED_DEPENDENCY` | A `ref` names a declared Card that doesn't exist | Declare that Card first, or fix the reference |
| `WYRD_VALA_409_BIFROST_FINGERPRINT_MISMATCH` | A table in `spec.tables` already exists with different columns | Keep the existing schema, or use a new table name |
| `WYRD_PERMISSION_403_DENIED_RBAC` | Your credential lacks `cards:write` | Use a credential that can declare Cards |
| `WYRD_LOADER_400_INVALID_ENVELOPE` | A file failed local validation; nothing was sent | Run `wyrd declare --check` and fix the file it names |

## Next

[Record a run and observations](/wyrd/build-and-verify/observe/record-a-run-and-observations/) against the declared Service.

# Record a run and observations

Page: /wyrd/build-and-verify/observe/record-a-run-and-observations/

> Pull your Service's bundle, record rows inside a run, verify or submit them to a Verifier, and read them back by run ID.

Pull and load the exact Service version you deployed, wrap each request in a run, record what each component saw and did, and hand it to a Verifier with `verify` or `submit`. Verifiers judge these runs, and every row points back to the Card version and run that produced it. This is the path for application code; to load or query tables directly, use the [Bifrost client](/wyrd/build-and-verify/observe/write-and-query-custom-data-with-bifrost/).

[Runs, observations, and retained evidence](/wyrd/understand/runs-observations-and-evidence/) explains the model behind these calls.

## Prerequisites

- The declared `support-desk` Service from [Verify your first agent](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/). Its Cards live in `examples/support-desk-app/service/`: the Service declares a `tickets` table with `question` and `answer` columns, binds `no-refund-promise` (one `answer` input) to itself, and binds `ticket-complete` (one `ticket` input) and `follows-policy` (one `letter` file) to its `agent` component.
- A credential bound to that Service version, so the server can attribute what it records. Against the local server from [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/), the saved settings work as they are, as in the quickstart. Elsewhere, a tenant administrator issues one:

  ```bash
  wyrd auth issue-key --kind Service --name support-desk --version 1.0.0 --space default
  ```

  The key prints once. Give it to the service as `WYRD_API_KEY`, alongside `WYRD_SERVER_URL`.
- The SDK for your language: `pip install "wyrd-ai[otel]"`, `npm install wyrd-ai`, or the `wyrd-ai` crate with its `otel` feature.

## 1. Pull the bundle

`wyrd pull` writes the Service and every Card it references, including model weights and datasets, into the directory you name. Do this at build or deploy time, not per request:

```bash
wyrd pull --space default --kind Service --name support-desk --version 1.0.0 \
  --output-dir ./.wyrd-bundle
```

Pull replaces an existing bundle only once the new one is complete, so a failed pull leaves the previous bundle usable. `wyrd get` with the same selector prints the Service's envelope only and writes nothing. The example apps pull from code instead, right after declaring; see step 4 of the [quickstart](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/#4-deploy-the-cards).

## 2. Load it and start Bifrost and telemetry

Once, at startup:

**Python**

```python title="desk.py"
self.client = client or WyrdClient()
self.state = WyrdState.from_path(BUNDLE, self.client)
self.state.start_bifrost()
# Spans export to Wyrd through the SDK's OTLP exporter; the Agents SDK's
# own traces become spans too, under the request's Run.
self.state.start_telemetry()
set_trace_processors([WyrdAgentsTraceProcessor()])
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let state = WyrdState::from_path_with(bundle, client.clone())?;
// Starts the buffered writer the ticket rows go through.
state.start_bifrost().await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="server.ts"
// WYRD_SERVER_URL and WYRD_API_KEY, else the settings `wyrd server dev` saved, say which server to use and who the app is.
const client = WyrdClient.connect();
// The declared Service, pulled by `npm run deploy`.
const state = WyrdState.fromPath(BUNDLE_DIR, { client });
await state.startBifrost(); // writes tickets to Bifrost
await state.startTelemetry(); // exports spans to Wyrd
```

`from_path` reads local files only. `start_bifrost` is the first server call: it connects the writer and fails at startup if the server is unreachable or your credential cannot write observations. Telemetry exports spans started inside a run with that run's ID. In Python and TypeScript it is `state.start_telemetry()` (`startTelemetry`). In Rust it is `wyrd_ai::otel::start_telemetry(&state)`, which returns a `Telemetry` handle you keep until shutdown; the Rust app starts it when it begins serving, in step 4.

## 3. Record, verify, and submit

Open a run, then call `observe` on it. Everything in one run shares a `run_id`. The app answers a question in a new run of the Service and records the ticket in the `tickets` table:

**Python**

```python title="desk.py"
run = self.state.run()
with run, tracer.start_as_current_span("support-desk.ask"):
    # These headers tie the gateway's record of the call to this Run.
    headers = {
        "wyrd-run-id": run.run_id,
        "wyrd-card-uid": str(self.state.card_ref("agent").uid),
    }
    model = OpenAIChatCompletionsModel(
        self.model, self.gateway.with_options(default_headers=headers)
    )
    agent = Agent(name="support-agent", model=model)
    result = await Runner.run(agent, self.template.replace("{{question}}", question))
    answer = str(result.final_output)
    run.observe.record(TICKETS, {"question": question, "answer": answer})
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let agent = self.state.agent(run.alias())?;
let ExecutionRoute::WyrdGateway { deployment } = &agent.card().spec.execution_route else {
    return Err(ApiError::internal(
        "the Agent does not route through the Wyrd gateway",
    ));
};
let prompt = &agent.prompt().metadata.prompt;
let rendered = prompt
    .render(&[("question", question)])
    .map_err(|_| ApiError::internal("the Agent's Prompt does not render"))?;
let mut body = serde_json::to_value(rendered)
    .map_err(|_| ApiError::internal("the rendered Prompt does not serialize"))?["body"]
    .take();
body["model"] = json!(format!("{deployment}/{}", prompt.model));
let client = self.state.client()?;
// These headers tie the gateway's record of the call to this Run.
let reply = reqwest::Client::new()
    .post(format!("{}/v1/chat/completions", client.server_url()))
    .bearer_auth(client.access_token().await?.expose())
    .header("wyrd-run-id", run.run_id().as_str())
    .header("wyrd-card-uid", run.subject_uid().as_str())
    .json(&body)
    .timeout(ANSWER_TIMEOUT)
    .send()
    .await
    .map_err(|_| ApiError::internal("the Wyrd gateway call failed"))?;
let status = reply.status();
let reply: Option<Value> = reply.json().await.ok();
if !status.is_success() {
    return Err(ApiError::refusal(status, reply.as_ref()));
}
let reply =
    reply.ok_or_else(|| ApiError::internal("the gateway reply could not be read"))?;
let answer = reply["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
    .as_str()
    .ok_or_else(|| ApiError::internal("the gateway reply carries no text"))?
    .to_owned();
run.observe()
    .record(
        "vala.datasets.tickets",
        &json!({ "question": question, "answer": answer }),
    )
    .await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="server.ts"
const wyrdRun = support.state.run();
// Spans started inside the scope carry the Run's ID.
return wyrdRun.scope(async () => {
  const text = await answer(support.gateway, support.state, wyrdRun, question);
  await wyrdRun.observe.record(TICKETS, { question, answer: text });
  return check(wyrdRun, text);
});
```

Then it runs the two model-free Verifiers and waits for their verdicts. `no-refund-promise` is bound to the Service, so it runs on the run itself. `ticket-complete` is bound to the agent, so it runs on `for_card("agent")`, the run's agent view, which shares the same `run_id`:

**Python**

```python title="desk.py"
return {
    "no-refund-promise": run.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", answer=ticket["answer"]),
    "ticket-complete": run.for_card("agent").observe.verify(
        "ticket-complete", ticket=ticket
    ),
}
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let run = desk.state.run();
let agent = run.for_card("agent")?;
let work = async {
    let answer = desk.answer(&agent, &body.question).await?;
    let promise = run
        .observe()
        .verify(
            "no-refund-promise",
            Inputs::named([("answer", Input::from(json!(answer)))]),
        )
        .await?;
    let ticket = json!({
        "question": body.question,
        "answer": answer,
        "order_id": body.order_id,
    });
    let complete = agent
        .observe()
        .verify(
            "ticket-complete",
            Inputs::named([("ticket", Input::from(ticket))]),
        )
        .await?;
    Ok::<_, ApiError>((answer, promise, complete))
};
let (answer, promise, complete) = run
    .scope(work.instrument(tracing::info_span!("support-desk.ask")))
    .await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="server.ts"
const ticket = { question, answer: text, order_id: orderId ?? null };
const [promise, complete] = await Promise.all([
  wyrdRun.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", { answer: text }),
  wyrdRun.forCard("agent").observe.verify("ticket-complete", { ticket }),
]);
```

`follows-policy` calls a model judge, so the app queues it on the agent's letter instead of waiting:

**Python**

```python title="desk.py"
execution = run.for_card("agent").observe.submit(
    "follows-policy", letter=verify.File(letter.encode(), filename="letter.md")
)
assert isinstance(execution, verify.Execution)  # Run evidence always queues one
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let submission = run
    .observe()
    .submit("follows-policy", letter_inputs(&letter))
    .await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="server.ts"
const letter = verify.File.bytes(new TextEncoder().encode(text), { filename: "letter.md" });
const inputs = { letter };
const submitted = await wyrdRun.forCard("agent").observe.submit("follows-policy", inputs);
if (submitted.kind !== "queued") throw new Error("follows-policy judges Run evidence, so submit queues it");
```

| Call | Does | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `record(table, row)` | Queues one row for a `vala.datasets` table | Nothing; the row is stored at the next flush |
| `verify(name, inputs)` | Runs a Verifier and waits for it | The verdict (`passed`, `failed`, or `inconclusive`) and one result per requirement |
| `submit(name, inputs)` | Queues a Verifier on the server | An execution whose `id` reads the result later |

`verify` and `submit` take a Verifier bound to the Card of the run or view you call them on, and one input per slot that Verifier declares: `answer` for `no-refund-promise`, `ticket` for `ticket-complete`, and the `letter` file for `follows-policy`. `verify.File` fills a file slot. A failed verdict is a normal return, not an error.

Read a submitted result back from any process, by its execution ID alone:

**Python**

```python title="app.py"
# Any process can pick a check up from its execution ID alone.
state = verify.Execution.connect(execution_id, request.app.state.desk.client).status()
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let state = Execution::connect_with(id, desk.state.client()?)
    .await?
    .status()
    .await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="server.ts"
const execution = await verify.Execution.connect(executionId, { client: support.client });
const { status, error, result } = await execution.status();
```

`status()` returns the execution's state without waiting; `wait` on the same execution blocks until it is final, up to the timeout you pass.

## 4. Shut down cleanly

Queued rows and spans are not stored yet. Shut down once when the process stops:

**Python**

```python title="app.py"
app.state.desk = Desk()
yield
# Flush buffered tickets and spans to Wyrd before exiting.
app.state.desk.state.shutdown()
```

**Rust**

```rust title="lib.rs"
let telemetry = start_telemetry(&self.state)?;
let state = self.state.clone();
let served = axum::serve(listener, self.router())
    .with_graceful_shutdown(stop)
    .await;
// Flush spans first, then drain buffered tickets, before exiting.
telemetry.shutdown()?;
state.shutdown().await?;
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="server.ts"
// Flush every span and row before exiting: shutdown flushes the provider startTelemetry installed, then drains the writer.
for (const signal of ["SIGINT", "SIGTERM"]) {
  process.on(signal, async () => {
    server.close();
    await state.shutdown();
    process.exit(0);
  });
}
```

`shutdown` sends everything still queued and returns once the server has it. A process killed without it can lose its last rows and spans. `flush` does the same without closing the writer, for tests and batch jobs. In Python and TypeScript, both first flush the tracer provider `start_telemetry` installed, and still drain the writer if that flush fails. In Rust, `WyrdState::shutdown` drains only the writer: call `shutdown()` on the `Telemetry` handle first, as above.

## 5. Read a run back

Every row a run produced carries its `run_id`, so one query joins the ticket to the request span, the gateway call, and each verdict:

**Python**

```python title="evidence.py"
SQL = """
```
